# CLAUDE.md

Project conventions for Claude (Anthropic CLI / agent sessions) working on this repository. Sessions inherit nothing across cold starts, so the durable rules live here.

**A recurring value across these conventions:** prefer the existing structure over indirection that narrows nothing — churn (renames, façades, per-module "engines", parallel counters/diagnostics) must earn its keep. Where that trade-off bites, the relevant section calls it out as the *bad-façade / namespace-churn trap*.

**Priority when anti-churn and consistency collide:** consistency wins when the inconsistency is *recurring and reader-facing* (every new reader re-pays it); anti-churn wins only when the change is *purely cosmetic* — a rename or reshuffle that removes no confusion. A persistent inconsistency is a real, compounding cost, not a cosmetic one. This leans consistency-first on purpose: the project is mature (low debt, high coverage), and churn is cheap on clean, well-tested code, so a consistency fix that disturbs the module-boundary baseline or a namespace is usually worth it.

**A name that encodes a value or a scope goes false when the value or the scope moves, and nothing reports it.** Before choosing a name, ask what would have to change for it to become false. When the answer is a number, a screen list or a sibling's spelling, the name borrows something it does not own: prefer the step over the pixel (`.ffc-mt-xl`, never `.ffc-mt-15`), the family over the screen, and the thing's own identity over its neighbour's (the table is `ffc_short_urls`; `ffc_url_shortener` is only an option-key and metabox-id prefix, and the pair costs a lookup every time).

**Two hard limits.** A name that is a **stored value** does not rename — `sindicato`, `rf_encrypted` and every `field_key` live in rows, and the language criterion below governs. And a rename rides a PR that already touches the file, because it is the most expensive change here to get wrong (the module-boundary baseline, `@covers`, alias mocks, the autoloader); a rename-only sweep is the churn the rule above refuses.

**A number in this file is a claim about a value something else owns, and it goes stale in silence**: the PR that changes the value edits the constant, never the paragraph here, and no gate reads this file. So **state the invariant, not the reading** — "the baseline blocks at zero" survives a shrink, "the baseline holds 3 entries" does not. Where a count carries the lesson, write it as history, in the past tense. Where a number stays, say what was counted, so the next reader can re-measure it. A count that drifts with every edit and carries nothing — a line count, a selector count — is deleted, not refreshed. When a figure looks stale, read the whole sentence: the damage is usually the conclusion built on it, and the fix is often to rewrite the claim and delete the figure.

**A cross-reference names the section, never numbers it** (`CLAUDE.md "Security & PII conventions"`), in the code and in this file alike, so a reordering breaks nothing. The audits behind these rules on names and numbers are in `docs/engineering/claude-md-maintenance.md`.

**Where a section lives.** A section goes in `.claude/rules/<topic>.md`, with a `paths:` list, when only work on files under those paths needs it: Claude Code loads the file when a session reads or edits a matching file, and `CLAUDE.md` keeps a short pointer that names the file and says to read it before that work starts from anywhere else. It stays here when it must be known before code is written anywhere: a prohibition, a rule a push can break, a convention that spans modules. A rule file without `paths:` loads in every session like this one, so its text belongs here instead. A reference to a section in another file names the file (`` `.claude/rules/stylesheets.md` "Theme" ``); `ClaudeRulesReferenceTest` holds every such reference, and every pointer and glob, to what exists.

**Language: every versioned artifact is in English; the conversation is not.** Code, comments, docblocks, assertion messages, `CHANGELOG.md`, commit messages, issue and PR titles and bodies, and the i18n source strings are English, with the translation in `languages/`, which is what keeps the plugin translatable into any language. The conversation with the maintainer is primarily Brazilian Portuguese, and that does not decide the language of what stays in the repository. `CommentLanguageTest` enforces the comment and source-string halves ("Quality gates and testing" → "Comment-language guard"); what it cannot reach is named there.

**Issue and PR bodies are the half nothing catches.** A body is composed in the flow of the conversation and inherits its language unless something interrupts, so the discipline belongs at the moment of writing it, not at review. Merged PR bodies stay as they are: each is a record of a moment, and editing them would make a PR title disagree with its own squash subject on `main`.

**When scanning for Portuguese, filter by what a word indicates.** A domain acronym inside an English sentence ("Search by name, email, ID or CPF/RF") is correct — `CPF` is a proper noun here, like `VAT` — while a functional word (`não`, `são`, `pelo`, `uma`) only appears in a Portuguese sentence. A narrow word list reports a tree clean when it is not.

**`ficha` is settled on Record** (#1280). Exactly two source strings keep "ficha" on purpose — one names the template kind, which is a stored value, and one records the hook family the rename came from — so grep for a third before assuming debt. The history of the language cleanup is in `docs/engineering/i18n-and-language.md`.

**The exception is a criterion, not a list: a domain term stays in Portuguese when renaming it would break the database or require a migration.** `rf_encrypted` / `rf_hash` / `rf_normalized` are real columns in a `CREATE TABLE`; `sindicato`, `acumulo_cargos`, `endereco_numero`, `email_institucional`, `termo_ciencia` and `nome_completo` are `field_key` values written into `ffc_custom_fields` *and* keys of the `data` JSON of every stored submission. Renaming those means migrating every install's rows, for a term like `RF` (*Registro Funcional*) that has no English equivalent an SME operator would recognise. Everything else renames — a method name, a class, a local variable touch no stored row, so `get_sindicato_options()` is not covered by the exception even though the field key it serves is. Expect that split to look odd in the diff (`get_union_options()` feeding `'field_key' => 'sindicato'`) and to need one line saying the key is the stored value; that is the honest shape, not an oversight.

## 1. Contributing workflow

### Pull-request workflow

The repository has **"Allow auto-merge"** enabled in Settings → General.
Use it on every PR — no manual squash + merge unless auto-merge fails.

**PR base branch:** by default, target `develop`, not `main`. The only PRs that target `main` are (1) the periodic release PR `develop → main` that consolidates the accumulated batch with a single version bump, and (2) hotfix PRs from `hotfix/*` branches when a critical bug needs to ship without waiting for develop's queue to consolidate. See "Develop branch workflow" below for the full mapping.

After `mcp__github__create_pull_request`:

1. `mcp__github__update_pull_request` with `draft: false` (auto-merge only fires on non-draft PRs).
2. `mcp__github__enable_pr_auto_merge` with `mergeMethod: SQUASH`. 
3. End your turn. GitHub merges as soon as every required check passes; `<github-webhook-activity>` fires the merge event back to the session.

Don't poll CI manually after step 2 unless the user asks. The webhook subscription delivers **failures + comments + the final merge event**; green completion is silent by design.

**Batch related work; gate the draft→ready flip.** Group trivially-related changes — especially docs-only (CHANGELOG / CLAUDE.md / comments) — into one PR; they gain nothing from the per-PR testes deploy and only multiply CI runs and rebase churn. Use **draft** to accumulate commits and keep the window short: open the PR late (work essentially done + locally green), rebase if `develop` moves under it, and treat a second forced rebase as the signal to finish or split. **Before flipping draft→ready + auto-merge:** if the PR completes a pre-agreed unit (a planned sprint/roadmap item with obvious done-criteria), go straight to ready + auto-merge; if the scope is ad-hoc or emerged mid-session — completeness not obvious from a plan — **confirm with the user first**, so follow-ups stay batched in the same PR instead of spawning a trickle of tiny PRs. No calendar deadline on drafts — the signal is drift (develop moving under the branch), not elapsed time.

**Split by diff size, then stop.** The reviewable unit is the diff, so split only when one diff would genuinely be unreadable. Where the work is one mechanical pass over many files, two large PRs beat four comfortable ones, because every extra PR on `[Unreleased]` costs a `CHANGELOG.md` conflict.

**Documentation travels with the change, in the same PR.** A PR that changes what an operator sees or configures — a screen, a setting, a default, a capability, a menu, an e-mail — updates the topic under `includes/settings/views/documentation/` that describes it, with its strings in the three catalogues. This is where drift is cheapest to prevent, while the author still knows what changed; the release cross-check below catches it after the fact. `DocumentationCoverageTest` guards the mechanical half (every tab and module has a topic, the index and the topic files agree); whether a topic tells the truth is not reachable by a test.

**The translated readme travels with `readme.txt`, in the same PR.** `languages/readme-pt_BR.txt` is what "View details" shows a pt_BR administrator. `PluginDetailsAssetsTest` holds it to `readme.txt` by structure only — the same tab sections, the same count of other sections, the same screenshot captions — and cannot see a sentence, so the discipline belongs to the PR that changes the English, and the release cross-check below reads the two side by side.

**Closing an issue — leave no false-positive checkboxes.** When an issue closes as `completed`, either tick every delivered box (`- [x]`) **or** leave a short closing comment that maps each delivered item to the PR that shipped it; an unticked box for shipped work reads as pending to a later scan. Legitimately-deferred boxes stay unticked, and the closing comment names them as deferred, so "unticked" is never ambiguous between *done* and *dropped*.

**`Closes #NNN` does not auto-close in this workflow — close feature issues by hand.** GitHub auto-closes a linked issue only when the PR merges into the repository's **default branch**, which is deliberately `main`, not `develop`. Close the issue manually, with the checkbox reconciliation above, as soon as its work lands on `develop`; do **not** wait for the release PR. Genuinely-future work (a removal scheduled releases out) correctly stays open.

### Issues, pull requests and the merge queue

The shape of an issue and a PR lives in the templates — `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` (bug, feature, task) and `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE.md` (plus `PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE/release.md`, reached with `?template=release.md`). They are the layout; this section is the rules around them, and it is not repeated there. The same standard holds in Total Mail Queue, Email Signature Generator and Institutional Email.

- **An issue before the PR.** Every PR names the issue it closes. Exempt, and only these: a trivial docs or chore change, a Dependabot PR, the `release: X.Y.Z` bump and the CHANGELOG SHA backfill. An agent opens the issue itself, in English, from the task template — the issue is where the problem and the acceptance criteria are written down before the diff argues for one answer.
- **Titles.** Issue: `Area: the problem in one sentence`. PR: `type(scope): summary`, with `type` one of `feat`, `fix`, `docs`, `test`, `refactor`, `chore` and `scope` the area — it becomes the squash subject on `develop`, so it is written for the log. Release titles keep their own shape (`.claude/rules/release-and-deploy.md` "Release PR").
- **Labels: one type, one area.** Type is `bug`, `enhancement`, `task`, `documentation` or `security`; area is an `area:` label mirroring `Core\PluginAreas`, plus `area:identity` and `area:infra`. `duplicate`, `invalid` and `wontfix` say why something closed unmerged, and `dependencies` / `composer` / `npm` / `github-actions` belong to Dependabot — its config applies them, so deleting one only makes it come back. **An agent cannot create a label**, only apply one that exists: a missing label is the maintainer's to create.
- **A PR carries the labels of the issue it closes.** The agent's tool opens a PR with no labels and cannot set them at creation, so the agent applies them as the next step, before marking it ready. Every issue and every PR carries its type and its area.
- **One merge at a time.** Only one PR is ready with auto-merge armed; every other one waits as a draft. After a merge the next PR takes `develop` by a **merge**, never a rebase, its conflicts are resolved — `CHANGELOG.md` keeps both bullets in heading order, `.mo` / `.l10n.php` are recompiled with `php .github/scripts/ffc-compile-translations.php`, never hand-edited — its touched tests run again, and only then is it flipped to ready and armed. PRs editing `[Unreleased]` and the catalogues conflict on every merge, and resolving each against the `develop` that has already moved is what keeps the resolution checkable.
- **After each merge.** The agent closes the issue by hand (`Closes` does not fire on `develop`, see above), ticking or naming each acceptance criterion.
- **Branches.** With Settings → General → "Automatically delete head branches" on, GitHub deletes a merged PR's branch. Whatever survives — a branch without a PR, a release or sync branch — the agent lists at the end of the batch for the maintainer to delete, since an agent cannot delete a ref ("Branch naming"); local worktrees the agent removes itself.

### Branch naming

Use `claude/<short-kebab-description>` for feature branches that target `develop`. Examples in main history: `claude/js-coverage-sprint-B-audience-smoke`, `claude/csv-import-normalize-cpf-rf`. Use `hotfix/<short-kebab-description>` when cutting an urgent fix from `main` (see `.claude/rules/release-and-deploy.md` "Hotfix flow"). Always go through a PR — the PR is what gets the commit through CI, which a direct push does not.

**What an agent's credential can do.** It creates and updates refs, including by force: the rulesets carry an admin bypass that the credential uses (`.claude/rules/release-and-deploy.md` "Branch protection"). So "go through a PR" is a rule to follow, never a wall that stops you.

**An agent cannot delete a ref at all.** `git push --delete` returns **HTTP 403** on any branch, feature branches included. Deleting a merged feature branch is the maintainer's to do.

### Develop branch workflow

Adopted v6.7.7 to decouple iteration cadence from production. Source domain (prod) only sees one version bump per batch; the testes domain runs `develop` HEAD and absorbs the per-PR churn.

#### Branch topology

```
main      ─o──────────────────────o────────────  ← PROD (source domain)
                                  ↑
                                  release PR
                                  with consolidated bump
develop   ─o─o─o─o─o─o─o─o─o─o─o─/             ← TESTES (testes domain)
           PR1 PR2 PR3 …                         each merge auto-deploys
```

- **`main`** — the production branch. Updated only by (1) the release PR `develop → main` (squash merge with the final bump + consolidated CHANGELOG entry) and (2) hotfix PRs `hotfix/* → main` when a critical bug bypasses the queue.
- **`develop`** — the integration branch. Default base for every feature PR. Each merge into `develop` triggers `.github/workflows/deploy-develop.yml`, which rsyncs the working tree to the testes server.
- **`hotfix/*`** — short-lived. Cut from `main`, merge back to `main`, then rebase `develop` on top of the new `main` (see `.claude/rules/release-and-deploy.md` "Hotfix flow").

#### Per-PR flow (the common case)

1. Feature branch `claude/<desc>` cut from `develop`.
2. PR targets `develop`. CI gates run identically to PRs against main.
3. **No `FFC_VERSION` bump in the feature PR.** Develop accumulates work under the existing `FFC_VERSION` until release time.
4. CHANGELOG entries go under the `[Unreleased]` section at the top of `CHANGELOG.md` — they stay there across multiple PRs.
5. Auto-merge enabled (SQUASH). Once merged, `deploy-develop.yml` pushes the new HEAD to the testes server within ~1 minute.

#### Dependabot PRs

Dependabot is configured with `target-branch: develop` for all three ecosystems (`composer`, `npm`, `github-actions`) in `.github/dependabot.yml`, so **version updates** open against `develop` correctly.

**Security updates are the exception:** GitHub always raises Dependabot *security* updates against the repository's default branch (`main`), ignoring `target-branch` — this is not configurable. The default branch is intentionally kept as `main` (changing it would have repo-wide side effects), so security-update PRs will keep being born against `main`.

**Rule — retarget to `develop`, and it is automatic (#2515):** whenever a Dependabot PR opens against `main` (in practice, always a security update), its base moves to `develop` with a one-line comment stating the reason (*every change funnels through `develop` and ships in the consolidated release PR, never as an out-of-band `main` commit*). `dependabot-automerge.yml` does it, in a step that runs **before** the one that turns on auto-merge: changing the base turns auto-merge off, so an auto-merge armed before the retarget would merge the PR straight into `main` and make the next release PR conflict on `package-lock.json`. **The step runs from `main`'s copy of the workflow**, because a `pull_request` workflow runs as the file stands on the PR's merge commit, which for a security update branched from `main` is `main`'s copy: a change to the step takes effect only once it ships in a release. The PR then rides the normal develop batch with auto-merge like any other; if its lockfile conflicts with `develop`, Dependabot rebases it.

**An agent cannot post a `@dependabot` command, and the failure is silent.** The agent's GitHub tooling injects separator characters into bot mentions, so the comment arrives mangled, Dependabot ignores it and nothing reports an error. **Do not retry the comment.**

What works instead, in this order:

1. **Check whether a rebase is needed at all.** It is only needed when the lockfile actually differs between `main` and `develop`: `git diff origin/main origin/develop -- package-lock.json composer.lock`. An empty diff means the PR's hunks apply to `develop` unchanged.
2. **If the PR is merely `behind`**, update the branch (`update_pull_request_branch`, the "Update branch" button). That is the whole fix in the common case.
3. **Only if the lockfile genuinely conflicts** does the rebase matter — ask the user to post `@dependabot rebase`, since `@dependabot recreate` from a mangled comment is not an option either.

**`develop` requires a branch to be up to date before merging.** So `behind` is the expected state for any PR that `develop` moved under: read `mergeable_state`, and treat `behind` as a step to take (step 2 above), never a state to wait out. This holds for every PR here, not only Dependabot's.

**Exception — genuine hotfix:** if the security fix is in a **runtime dependency** (shipped inside the plugin, not dev/CI tooling) *and* is severe enough to ship to production immediately, treat it as a hotfix (`hotfix/* → main`) instead of retargeting, then sync develop per `.claude/rules/release-and-deploy.md` "Sync `develop` with `main`". Dev/CI-only deps (`vitest`, `@vitest/coverage-v8`, `undici`, `js-yaml`, PHPStan, etc.) never qualify — they always ride the develop batch.

**That exception is unreachable through Dependabot today.** The plugin ships **zero** managed third-party runtime dependencies: `composer.json`'s `require` is `php` alone, `package.json`'s `dependencies` is empty, and `.distignore` drops both `/vendor` and `/node_modules` from the zip. So every package Dependabot can see is dev/CI-only, and the decision is mechanical — check `require` / `dependencies` and the answer falls out.

The flip side is the part that matters: **the code that actually ships is invisible to Dependabot.** The hand-vendored bundles in `libs/js/` — each named `<library>-<version>.<ext>` with its licence beside it as `<library>-<version>.LICENSE.txt`, and listed in `VendoredBundleInventoryTest` — are enqueued at runtime, inside the distributable, and in no manifest. A CVE in any of them will never open a PR here; it has to be noticed by a person, so what is running has to be readable off the tree (#1202).

**That is why the version lives in the filename and the path is built from the constant**, never from a literal: `FFC_PLUGIN_URL . 'libs/js/jspdf-' . FFC_JSPDF_VERSION . '.umd.min.js'`. The two halves then cannot drift — bumping `FFC_JSPDF_VERSION` without renaming the file 404s the script, which breaks PDF generation loudly. With a literal path the constant is only the `?ver=` argument, so the same bump silently serves the **old** bundle under a new cache key. One thing deliberately stays untouched: a vendored bundle's own `//# sourceMappingURL=` comment still names the upstream filename, because editing it would break byte-for-byte verification against upstream, which is the reason to vendor at all.

#### Release, hotfix, sync and deploy — `.claude/rules/release-and-deploy.md`

The release PR (`develop → main`), the hotfix flow, syncing `develop` with `main`, the branch rulesets, the testes deploy and its post-deploy smoke are in `.claude/rules/release-and-deploy.md`. It loads by itself when a session reads or edits a file under `.github/workflows/` or `.github/scripts/`; **read it before any release, hotfix, sync of `develop`, tag or deploy work**, which usually starts from a request rather than from one of those files. Two rules hold before you open it: **an agent never pushes a release tag** — it surfaces the tagging sequence for the maintainer to run, because the tag publishes the production zip — and **the `develop → main` PR stays draft until the maintainer confirms the production deploy**.

### Versioning

Three places carry the plugin version and must stay in sync:

1. `ffcertificate.php` plugin header — `* Version: X.Y.Z`. Parsed by WordPress core BEFORE PHP runs, so it must be a literal string.
2. `ffcertificate.php` PHP constant — `define( 'FFC_VERSION', 'X.Y.Z' )`. Source of `?ver=…` on every `wp_enqueue_*` call.
3. `readme.txt` `Stable tag: X.Y.Z`. Parsed by WordPress.org before PHP runs; also a literal string.

When changing the version, update all three in the same commit. `PluginIdentityTest` fails when they disagree, when the released version has no `## [X.Y.Z]` section in `CHANGELOG.md`, and when the PHP or WordPress floor in the header differs from `readme.txt`, `composer.json` (`require` and `config.platform`) or the `testVersion` / `minimum_wp_version` that `phpcs.xml.dist` judges the code against.

#### Patch vs. cache-bust-only releases

- A "real" patch release (any source-code change) consumes the next patch number: `6.6.2 → 6.6.3`.
- A **cache-bust-only release** (no functional change — exists purely to rotate the `?ver=…` asset cache key after a prior PR shipped an updated `.min.js` / `.min.css` without bumping the version) uses a 4th segment appended to the prior version: `6.6.2 → 6.6.2.1`. The next cache-bust sibling of the same minor would be `6.6.2.2`, and so on. WordPress's `version_compare()` and the plugin update flow both handle 4-segment versions without special-casing.
- Reason for the convention: a cache-bust release carries no new user-visible behavior, only a key rotation. Burning a real patch number on it would imply meaningful changes that aren't there.

#### When to bump

The trigger has not changed — bundled-asset changes still rotate the cache key. What changed with the develop branch workflow is **where the bump lands**:

- **PRs targeting `main`** (release PR `develop → main`, hotfix PR `hotfix/* → main`): bump `FFC_VERSION` in the same PR. The release PR consolidates every `assets/**/*.min.js`, `assets/**/*.min.css`, `templates/**.php`, and `languages/*.l10n.php` / `.mo` change from the develop batch under one version. Hotfix PRs bump their own patch number.
- **PRs targeting `develop`**: do **not** bump. Develop sits at the last released version (the cache key on the testes domain stays stable across the batch), and the testes site sidesteps it through the file-time versioning `SCRIPT_DEBUG=true` turns on (see `.claude/rules/release-and-deploy.md` "Deploy to testes"). Bumping per-PR on develop would consume version numbers that have no production analog.

The "Verify minified assets are up to date" CI job catches build freshness on both bases but does NOT enforce the version bump — that's still a human discipline on the release PR.

### CHANGELOG conventions

`CHANGELOG.md` follows Keep a Changelog. Per change:

- One entry under the top `[Unreleased]` section, grouped by heading (`Added` / `Changed` / `Fixed` / `Security` / `Removed` / `Deprecated`). Entries stay in `[Unreleased]` across PRs until the release PR renames the heading (`.claude/rules/release-and-deploy.md` "Release PR").
- **Always cite the issue/PR** (`(#NNN)` / `#NNN`). Every `[Unreleased]` bullet must carry a reference — the linked PR holds the granular detail.
- **Append the bullet at the END of its heading's list, never at a fixed point inside it.** Two concurrent branches still collide on `[Unreleased]` — two appends land on the same line — but the resolution is then always *keep both, in either order*, with nothing to judge. Order of arrival has no value anyway, because the release PR condenses the section by story.
- **No internal roadmap codenames** in the prose — no "Sprint N", "phase N", or letter-codes (`A6`, `B3`, `E5`, …). Describe the change itself and keep entries concise (one tight paragraph, not a wall of class-by-class text).
- Ordinary words that happen to look like codes — "A4" (paper size), "four-phase flow" (literal steps) — are fine; the rule targets roadmap taxonomy only.
- **Aim for ≤300 characters per bullet.** A *soft* target, not a CI gate — a bullet may exceed it when the detail genuinely earns the length (a breaking-change banner, a subtle regression), but prefer trimming first: the linked PR holds the granular detail.

  **Condense the section before the release PR when it needs it.** Two cheap signals say it does: a median bullet length well above the 300 target, and duplicate headings (`### Added` twice), the tell that batches were appended without anyone re-reading the section. Condense **by story, not by PR**, then prove nothing was lost by checking programmatically that every issue that delivered work is still cited; references that leave should only be precedents quoted in prose. `release.yml` publishes that section verbatim as the **public Release notes**, so it is what the user reads. The measurements behind this are in `docs/engineering/workflow-history.md`.

### What not to do

- Do not amend or rewrite published commits on `main`. On `develop`, force-push is permitted only for the documented sync-with-main rebase (`.claude/rules/release-and-deploy.md` "Sync `develop` with `main`") — never to rewrite arbitrary history.
- Do not skip hooks (`--no-verify`) or signing.
- Do not bypass the coverage floor — bump it forward or restore the lost coverage. Never lower it — the sole exception is an honest re-measure after deleting covered **product** code (never tests); see "CI gates".
- Do not add new untested code paths in a coverage-aware PR; either cover them in the same PR or document the deferral.
- Do not target `main` directly from a feature PR. The only PRs that base on `main` are the release PR (`develop → main`) and hotfix PRs (`hotfix/* → main`).
- Do not bump `FFC_VERSION` in a **feature** PR that targets `develop` — the bump belongs to the release. (The lone exception is the dedicated `release: X.Y.Z` bump PR an agent uses to land the bump on `develop` when it can't direct-push; see `.claude/rules/release-and-deploy.md` "Release PR" → "Landing the bump on `develop`".)

## 2. Quality gates and testing

### CI gates (all gating, enforced on `main` and `develop`)

- PHP: PHPStan (level 8) · Row shapes (PHPStan level 9, reported for the classes that read `$wpdb` rows) · WPCS · PHPUnit (8.3/8.4) · PHPUnit in reverse order (8.4, see below) · Coverage ≥ floor (clover, env `COVERAGE_FLOOR_LINES` in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`).
- JS / CSS: ESLint (zero-error) · Stylelint (zero-error) · Vitest + coverage ≥ floor (env `JS_COVERAGE_FLOOR_LINES` in `.github/workflows/lint.yml`).
- Misc: CodeQL (javascript) · Composer audit · Review dependency changes · Verify minified assets are up to date · **Fresh install (PHP 8.3)**, on the latest WordPress and on the declared floor — see below.

**The suite runs in three orders, and only two of them gate (#2197).** The shards run it in the declared order. `PHPUnit (PHP 8.4, reverse order)` runs the whole suite in one process with `--order-by=reverse` and gates, because the suite must pass reversed (#2123). It is one process, not a shard, because reversing a subset only reorders within it. `.github/workflows/suite-order.yml` runs it with `--order-by=random` on every push to `develop`, daily and on demand, and never on a pull request: it is an **alarm, not a gate**, because a fixed order can only ever show the dependencies it happens to break, while a random one finds new ones at a moment unrelated to the change in front of it. Its seed is in the log; replay a failure with `vendor/bin/phpunit --order-by=random --random-order-seed=<seed>`, open an issue with the seed and the failing pair, and fix the test that reads state it did not set. Whether the random run should gate is decided later, from its record.

The same gates run on PRs to `develop` and on the release PR `develop → main`. Develop must stay deployable to the testes site, so we don't relax gates there — a green develop is the precondition for opening the next release PR.

The coverage floors are ratcheted upward in the PR that delivers the gain — never lowered. The comment block above each `*_FLOOR_LINES` keeps the audit trail.

**One exception — code deletion.** Removing well-covered **product** code (never tests) can legitimately drop the line-% because high-coverage lines left the denominator — that is not a regression to restore. When a deletion PR lowers the measured coverage, an honest re-measure of the floor down to the new figure is allowed, provided the `*_FLOOR_LINES` comment block records the deleting PR and the new baseline. This is the *only* case the floor may move down; deleting or weakening tests to relax it never qualifies.

**The floor rule is shared by the four plugins** (Free Form Certificate, Total Mail Queue, Email Signature Generator, Institutional Email) and by Site PWA: **a floor is the highest of 90%, the measured figure minus 5 points, and its current value.** So it is never below 90%, never more than 5 points behind what is measured, and never lowered except by the deletion re-measure above. The 5-point buffer absorbs v8/clover run-to-run jitter and the sharded phpcov merge, which runs a little under a single-process measure, so the gate does not flake on fractional swings. Raise the floor in the PR that delivers the gain, and only once the figure CI measured is above it — never above the lowest run actually observed. It applies to both `COVERAGE_FLOOR_LINES` (PHP) and `JS_COVERAGE_FLOOR_LINES` (JS).

### The guards

Every guard below runs inside the PHPUnit gate above, except the two that need a database and live in the `fresh-install` job. Each exists because a defect had already shipped. What each one cost to find, and the measurements behind its design, are in `docs/engineering/guards.md` (schema guards: `docs/engineering/schema-and-migrations.md`); read a guard's entry there before changing its scan.

Two properties they share, and both are load-bearing. Every one carries a **self-check that fails when its own scan collapses** — an empty result must never read as clean (#1071 / #1094). And every one **sees presence, never truth**: a wrong reason in an allowlist passes, an assertion against the mock that supplies the value passes. Crossing the boundary a guard mocks is what the `fresh-install` job does for schema, and what a render does for CSS.

**A seam is worth a guard by what its contract is made of, not by how much it hurts (#1525).** A number or a name declared on both ends — an `accepted_args`, an AJAX action, an option key — is cheap to guard and worth it (`ZeroArgHookArityTest`, `AjaxWiringTest`). The shape of an object crossing PHP and JavaScript is not: a regex cannot follow JS scope, and a scan at that false-positive rate gets allowlisted into silence. The localized-payload and `data-ffc-*` seams were both measured and came back with no live defect; do not re-run either census on a hunch.

**A self-check is worth what it is tight to, and a floor loosens on its own as the population grows (#1428).** Reach for these shapes in this order:

1. **PREFERRED, when a non-empty frozen register exists — an exact comparison against it** (`assertSame` against the baseline). A shrink-only ratchet is itself the detector: a scan that loses files loses a baselined entry. A register driven to zero gives this up and owes an explicit self-check instead.
2. **PREFERRED, when there is no register — an independent recount** by a different traversal (`scandir` against `RecursiveIteratorIterator`, or against `glob`), as `ActivatorSqlTest` does. Where the scan filters, the recount repeats the filter and the two can drift; prefer it anyway, because a drifting recount fails while a decaying floor goes quiet.
3. **ACCEPTABLE, only when repeating the filter would be dishonest — a floor stated as a share of an independently counted population.** It has constant slack rather than growing slack; never use it to soften a comparison that could have been exact.
4. **LAST RESORT — naming a single deep member** the scan can least afford to miss (`PhpcsSuppressionTest` names `uninstall.php`). When that member legitimately leaves, the guard fails and asks to be re-pointed.

**NEVER a bare floor.** An absolute floor decays as the population grows past it. A share derived from the scan's own count detects nothing, because halving the scan halves numerator and denominator together. An audit that halves a population to test any of this must prove the population actually shrank: a one-element `glob` halved is still itself. Re-run that census as a one-off when the guard population grows, never as a gate.

#### Module-boundary guard (#563 B3)

`tests/Unit/ModuleBoundaryTest.php` freezes the cross-module dependency graph of `includes/` (a "module" = the first namespace segment after `FreeFormCertificate\`; an edge = module A referencing `FreeFormCertificate\B\…`) against the committed baseline `tests/fixtures/module-boundary-baseline.php`. The graph is a **ratchet that can only shrink**: a *new* edge fails (new cross-module coupling — justify it or route through a facade); a *removed* edge also fails (coupling eliminated — lock the win in). After an intentional change, regenerate + review the diff: `FFC_UPDATE_BOUNDARY_BASELINE=1 vendor/bin/phpunit --filter ModuleBoundary`. Never regenerate just to make a red guard green without understanding the new edge.

#### Fresh-install gate (#994)

`.github/workflows/ci.yml` → job `fresh-install` installs a throwaway WordPress onto a MariaDB service, activates the plugin into an **empty** database, and runs `.github/scripts/fresh-install-check.php`. It is the only gate that sees a *fresh activation*: the post-deploy smoke runs against an established install, where a `CREATE` that stopped working is invisible. It runs twice — on the latest WordPress (`Fresh install (PHP 8.3)`, a required check name that must not change) and on the newest patch of the declared floor (`Fresh install (PHP 8.3, WordPress floor)`, read from `Requires at least`), so moving the floor moves the test.

The comparison against `uninstall.php` runs **both ways**: every declared object must exist, and every `ffc_*` table and option that exists must be declared. The job then deletes the plugin with the Danger Zone opt-in on and asserts the footprint is zero, so `uninstall.php` is an **enforced manifest**. `.github/scripts/ffc-uninstall-manifest.php` parses it as text (never includes it — that would run the uninstaller), and the post-deploy smoke reads the same parse, so adding a table or option to `uninstall.php` covers it everywhere.

**It runs locally too, minus its last step.** The container's MariaDB (`root` / `root`): install a throwaway WordPress with WP-CLI, symlink this checkout into its `wp-content/plugins`, activate, and run `fresh-install-check.php <wp> uninstall.php activate`, `dbdelta-idempotence-check.php <wp>` and `identity-index-invariant-check.php <wp>`. **Never run the job's uninstall step against a symlinked checkout**: `wp plugin uninstall` deletes the plugin directory, which is the repository. The container's MariaDB is 10.11 where CI pins 11.8, so a local pass is evidence, not the gate.

**The MariaDB image is a deliberate pin** to the host's version, which the post-deploy smoke prints (`VERSION()` and `@@sql_mode`) on every deploy; move the pin when the smoke shows the host moved, never to a familiar LTS. The gate is not a substitute for the smoke: only the host has the provider's PHP SAPI and wp-config.

The cheap half of the same defect class runs with no database in `tests/Unit/ActivatorSqlTest.php`, which enforces two `dbDelta` rules on every `CREATE TABLE` literal: **no semicolon before the final one** (`dbDelta()` splits its input on `;`, truncating the statement), and **every line a column or key definition** (a blank line or an SQL comment is read as a column and becomes a malformed `ALTER` on every run against an existing table).

#### dbDelta idempotence gate (#1087)

A step in the `fresh-install` job replays every `CREATE TABLE` through `dbDelta()` against the table it just created from that very statement. When statement and stored schema disagree in a way the statement can never satisfy, `dbDelta` re-ALTERs on every run that reaches it, and nothing else sees it. The statements come from `.github/scripts/ffc-create-statements.php`, shared with `ActivatorSqlTest`, and the gate aborts on an empty scan, a count that diverges from a wider net, or a table name it cannot resolve. **It blocks at zero**: a change it reports is a change to fix, never a line to add. Diagnosis needs the database, so on failure the gate dumps `SHOW CREATE TABLE` for the disagreeing statements; there is no way to reproduce it locally.

Three rules it enforces, each the opposite of what it looks like:

- **Write the display width.** MariaDB stores `int(10) unsigned` and compares textually, and WP core's `dbDelta` ignores a width-only difference on MySQL 8.0.17+ but *not* on MariaDB. `int(10)` is correct on both, and it is what WP core writes; do not "tidy" it to `int unsigned`.
- **Declare `longtext`, not `json`.** MariaDB implements `json` as `LONGTEXT` plus a CHECK, so a `json` column never matches. Nothing in the plugin uses a native JSON function; every read is `json_decode` in PHP.
- **Declare the index the code actually creates.** `Activator::upgrade_auth_code_unique_constraints()` converts `auth_code` to `UNIQUE INDEX uq_auth_code`, so a declared plain `KEY auth_code` never survives — the same shape as `validation_code` in the self-scheduling tables.

#### Schema-agreement guard (#1087)

`tests/Unit/SchemaAgreementTest.php` covers schema duplication without a database. **Within one file:** a `CREATE TABLE` and an `add_columns_if_missing()` call must name the same columns, because a fresh install gets the first and an upgraded install the second. **Across files:** where a table is declared by more than one class, every declaration must name the same columns and the same key names. The current list of such tables lives in the guard's own docblock, not here. It compares **names, not types** (the sources spell types differently by construction) and reads the statements through `.github/scripts/ffc-create-statements.php`.

#### Vacuous-test ratchet (#997)

`tests/Unit/AssertionCoverageTest.php` fails when a *new* test method verifies nothing — no Mockery/Brain\Monkey expectation and no assertion beyond a literal `assertTrue( true )`. The register `tests/fixtures/vacuous-tests-baseline.php` is a ratchet that can only shrink, and it is closed at one entry, kept deliberately with the reason in the test (`PluginActivationSmokeTest::test_foreign_key_migration_composes_when_version_stale` has no stronger observable without a database). An entry added to it is a decision to argue in the test. Regenerate after an intentional change with `FFC_UPDATE_VACUOUS_BASELINE=1 vendor/bin/phpunit --filter AssertionCoverage`.

**The way to prove a guard test is real is to delete the check it guards and confirm the test now fails**; a test that asserts the right thing for the wrong reason passes any static checker. Two things to know. `Functions\expect( 'wp_mail' )->once()` and `shouldNotReceive()` are real assertions, so the guard's expectation list must stay in sync with the idioms in use. And it sees presence, never strength: an assertion against a mock that supplies the very value under test passes it.

#### AJAX wiring guard

`tests/Unit/AjaxWiringTest.php` cross-checks, statically, that every registered `wp_ajax_*` handler is referenced somewhere other than its own registrar, that every `action` the client asks for is registered (on `wp_ajax_*`, `admin_post_*` or `admin_action_*`), and that every `get_option( 'ffc_*' )` key has a write path. It targets the "built but never wired" class (#935, #936).

**Registration has two idioms**, the literal `add_action( 'wp_ajax_ffc_x', … )` and the endpoint-class `add_action( 'wp_ajax_' . self::AJAX_ACTION, … )`, and both are resolved. **The client names an action in at least six shapes** — a `FFC.request` argument, an `action:` key, an `'action=…'` query fragment, a `FormData.append` pair, a hidden input's `value`, and a `wp_localize_script` payload carrying the constant — so direction A matches the bare token, deliberately loosely; direction B matches precise request positions, because a loose match there would flag nonce names and capability slugs. It proves only that both ends exist and agree on a name. Exceptions go in the `KNOWN_*` allowlists **with the reason inline**; an action that merely lost its caller does not belong there — delete the handler.

#### CSS namespace ratchet (#1152)

`tests/Unit/CssNamespaceAnchorTest.php` freezes the selectors in `assets/css/*.css` that name nothing the plugin owns. The baseline is **empty** and the ratchet only shrinks: a new anchorless selector fails, and so does a baselined one that gained an anchor. `test_no_stylesheet_publishes_a_new_anchorless_selector()` scans every sheet on every run; an entry added back to the baseline is a decision to defend. `:root` is the one allowlisted entry: it is *how* a custom property is declared, and every property under it is `--ffc-*`.

**An anchor is the wrong fix for a name that must be unique.** An id anchored inside a container still sits in the document, so a theme declaring `#tab-profile` breaks `getElementById`, `aria-controls` and the event delegation; the fix is a rename. Look for the house convention before inventing one (`ffc-tabnav-<key>` / `ffc-tabpanel-<key>`).

Mechanics of the scan: count **selectors, not classes** (a compound like `.appointment-status.status-pending` exposes one name); mind the token boundary (`a[href^="#ffc-separator-"]` is anchored although `#` precedes `ffc`); the scanner is quote-aware (`img[src^="data:image/png;base64"]` carries a `;`) and skips `@keyframes` steps. It does not see inline CSS printed from PHP, `style=""` attributes, or a class declared bare in two sheets — that last one is `StylesheetOwnershipTest`'s job.

#### Page-scope guard (#1184)

`tests/Unit/AdminPageScopeTest.php` fails when a `div.wrap` the plugin prints does not carry `ffc-admin-page` plus exactly one registered `ffc-page-<slug>`, when a registered screen class is emitted nowhere, or when a `NESTED` exception stops matching a real `wrap`. It proves only that the anchor is *there*, never that a rule reads it; that is `CssNamespaceAnchorTest`'s job. The convention and the screen map are in `.claude/rules/stylesheets.md` "Page scope on the admin `wrap`".

#### Component-ownership guard (#1162)

`tests/Unit/StylesheetOwnershipTest.php` fails when a class is declared **bare** — `.ffc-x { }`, no ancestor and no second class — in two sheets with **no dependency edge between them**, in either direction, direct or transitive. Without that edge the winner is enqueue order, which is the order modules are wired in `Loader`, so moving two bootstrap lines repaints a screen; and the result is a **merge** of both rules, not "the later one wins". Pairs that cannot coexist on one screen go in `ALLOWED` with the reason, because that impossibility lives in the enqueue gates, which this scan does not read. `BASELINE` is empty and the gate blocks at zero; the fix for a collision is a module-specific name (`ffc-appointment-status-*`, `ffc-audience-status-*`).

Mechanics for anyone extending it. One handle can be enqueued with different dependency lists at different sites, and the scan unions them, because what matters is whether the edge is declared anywhere. The extractor reads **top-level arguments**, not `explode( ',', … )`, because an inner comma (`dirname( __DIR__, 1 )`) cuts the list in the wrong place, and it resolves `self::HANDLE_CSS` against the file's own constants. `test_every_stylesheet_is_reachable_through_an_enqueue()` stops either failure from passing as clean; `ffc-appointment-cancellation.css` is the one sheet with no handle, because its handler prints the `<link>`s itself. The CSS parser is shared with the namespace ratchet through `tests/Support/CssSelectors.php`, so two guards measuring the same sheets cannot disagree about what a selector is.

#### Suppression guards (#1027, #1035)

`tests/Unit/PhpstanSuppressionTest.php` fails on a `@phpstan-ignore-next-line` (it suppresses *every* error on the line — the identifier after it is only a comment; only `@phpstan-ignore <id>` filters), on one naming no identifier, and on one with no reason. `tests/Unit/PhpcsSuppressionTest.php` fails on a bare annotation, one with no `-- reason` (or one under 15 characters — a floor against "ok", never a quality bar), and on the two structural defects below.

**PHPCS annotations are a flat on/off switch per sniff, not a stack.** A `phpcs:enable X` anywhere in a file turns X back on for the rest of it, whoever turned it off, so an inner disable/enable pair silently ends an enclosing file-level `disable`. When an inner pair names a sniff an outer disable already covers, drop it from the inner pair.

**`WordPress.DB.DirectDatabaseQuery` is disabled at file level in the repositories, activators and migrations, and that is scope-gated.** They query the plugin's own `ffc_*` tables, for which WordPress has no API. The disable is honest only while *every* table the file touches is `ffc_*`; `test_file_level_direct_query_disables_only_cover_plugin_tables()` enforces that, so a `wp_posts` / `wp_users` / `wp_usermeta` query in one of those files fails CI. Use the WP API or per-line annotations; `CORE_TABLE_EXCEPTIONS` is for an unavoidable reference (`MigrationForeignKeys` must name `wp_users`), with the reason inline.

**Neither guard sees deadness.** Deadness is measured, out of CI: **neutralise** every annotation in place by rewriting the sniff it names to one that cannot fire — **never** rename the `phpcs:` / `@phpstan-` token, which turns it into an ordinary comment and trips `Squiz.Commenting.InlineComment` — then re-run the tool and map what surfaces back to the annotations covering it. Verify by the gate, never by the classifier.

Parsing facts for anyone writing tooling over these: an own-line `phpcs:ignore` covers **its own line and the next one**; a `//` comment ends at `?>` (and a sniff list at `*/`), or the close tag is read as a sniff name; some annotations are the **trailing form, on the same line as code**, so deleting the line deletes the statement; and prose that merely mentions the token inside a docblock sentence is not a directive — only a token that opens its comment counts.

#### Comment-language guard (#1260)

`tests/Unit/CommentLanguageTest.php` fails when a comment line in a **PHP, JS or CSS** file (minified files excepted), or an i18n **source string**, carries **two distinct** Portuguese function words. It is the enforcement half of this file's opening language rule. Two design decisions carry it. *Two distinct words, not one*: a single word collides with English and code (`.com`, `DoS`), while two essentially never co-occur in an English technical sentence, so the list can stay wide. *Quoted is mentioned, not used*: a backticked or quoted span is stripped before matching, which is why `ALLOWED` ships empty. Every word is in the list for being Portuguese, never for catching one corpus's block — an English word that happens to sit on a Portuguese line is the "dictionary describes itself" trap.

A `/* … */` block in a stylesheet is read across every line it spans, and a self-check recounts `assets/css/` with a second traversal. What it does not see, deliberately: a single Portuguese word, a sentence with one Portuguese word used twice, `languages/` (that is the translation), `CHANGELOG.md`, commit messages and PR bodies — the PR-body half is disciplined at the moment of writing, because nothing else catches it.

#### Catalogue-agreement guard (#1266)

`tests/Unit/TranslationCatalogueAgreementTest.php` compares the three files in `languages/` by `(msgctxt, msgid)` in both directions: every **translated** `.po` entry must appear with the same value in the `.mo` and the `.l10n.php`, and neither compiled catalogue may carry an entry the `.po` does not; plurals compare form by form. Every supported WordPress prefers the `.l10n.php`; the `.mo` is still what WordPress loads when the `.l10n.php` is missing or forced off through `translation_file_format`, and what translation tools read.

**Recompile, never hand-edit.** After changing the `.po`, `php .github/scripts/ffc-compile-translations.php` writes the `.mo` (GNU gettext's `msgfmt --check`) and the `.l10n.php` from the same `PoCatalogue` reader this guard uses. The `.l10n.php` is `wp i18n make-php`'s shape byte for byte — check that again with WP-CLI when the compiler changes.

**Parse a file with its own language where you can**: the `.l10n.php` is read by **including** it, because it is a side-effect-free `return array()`. `uninstall.php` is parsed as text because including it would run the uninstaller — the rule is *include when the file does nothing*. Two key traps: the `.mo` keys a plural as `msgid \0 msgid_plural` while `.l10n.php` keys it by `msgid` alone, and a multi-line literal's `msgstr ""` opens a continuation rather than declaring an empty string.

#### Source-coverage guard (#1284)

`tests/Unit/TranslationSourceCoverageTest.php` compares the literal i18n calls in the source against the catalogue, both ways: **A**, every source string has a *translated* entry in the `.po` and the `.pot`, blocking at zero (an empty entry fails too: `msgfmt` omits it and pt_BR renders the English source); **B**, every entry has a call site, a shrink-only ratchet whose register separates the structural (the plugin header is a comment) from the debt, each entry naming what replaced it.

The extractor (`tests/Support/I18nCalls.php`) must read `T_NAME_FULLY_QUALIFIED` beside `T_STRING`, because `\__( … )` is one token carrying the backslash; a canary pins that shape. `PoCatalogue::read()` (`tests/Support/PoCatalogue.php`) returns an ordered **list**, not a keyed map, so a duplicate `msgid` fails instead of vanishing, and it **refuses an entry with no `msgstr` line** instead of reading it as empty.

#### Schema-reachability guard (#1311)

`tests/Unit/ActivatorSchemaGuardTest.php` also fails when a table declared under `includes/` has no declarer the `Loader` names. **`Activator::activate()` runs on plugin activation and nothing else performs one** — not an in-place WordPress update, not the rsync deploy — so a schema reachable only from there exists on fresh installs and on no upgraded one, while the `fresh-install` job stays green. **The rule is per TABLE, not per class**, which lets it block at zero with no allowlist: a one-shot migration may stay unwired while the tables it declares are creatable through a wired activator.

**Healing the schema is not re-running activation.** `UserDashboardActivator::maybe_migrate()` heals its two tables and nothing else, because its `create_tables()` also creates the dashboard page and registers a role — re-running those on every release would resurrect a page an administrator deleted. When wiring a new module, take the schema half only.

#### Schema-revision register (#2430)

**A schema change ships with a revision bump.** Every class that heals a schema on a request gates it on its own `SCHEMA_REVISION` and records it in `SCHEMA_REVISION_OPTION`, written only after the steps succeed and declared in `uninstall.php`. `FFC_VERSION` is not that gate: `develop` keeps the released version for a whole batch, so a schema change merged behind it would not reach the testes site until the release. `FFC_VERSION` stays the gate only for what really is per release.

`tests/Unit/SchemaRevisionRegisterTest.php` holds a register in `tests/fixtures/schema-revision-register.php`: per class that declares `SCHEMA_REVISION_OPTION`, its revision and a fingerprint of the schema its file declares (`tests/Support/SchemaRevisions.php` reads the DDL literals and the literal arguments of the schema helpers, so a comment or the logic around them moves nothing). A changed fingerprint with the same revision fails before the merge; a new revision fails until the register is regenerated with `FFC_UPDATE_SCHEMA_REVISION_REGISTER=1 vendor/bin/phpunit --filter SchemaRevisionRegister`. Any other file under `includes/` that declares schema names its owning class in `OWNERS` or its reason in `EXEMPT`. The same support class gives `ActivatorSchemaGuardTest` and `LoaderCapabilitiesTest` the current value of every revision option. It sees the text, never the database: a column assembled from variables, or a step left outside the gated chain, passes it.

#### Inline-style ratchet (#1837)

`tests/Unit/InlineStyleTest.php` freezes every place the plugin writes CSS outside a stylesheet — a `style=` attribute in PHP, a template or a JS string, a `<style>` element, `wp_add_inline_style()`, a CSS attributes array (`'style' => 'margin: 12px 0;'`), a jQuery `.css()` setter and a `.style` assignment — per file, each with its reason, a ratchet both ways. The scan is `tests/Support/InlineStyles.php` and reads comment-stripped source, so a docblock that mentions `style=` is not an occurrence. Two things it leaves out on purpose: a script toggling `display` (a static `style="display:none"` in markup still counts), and the three template directories that are inline by design, named in `EXCLUDED_DIRS` with their reasons. Its self-check is the independent recount: `glob()` / `scandir()` against the recursive iterator, the PHP occurrences again through `php_strip_whitespace()`, and the JS ones through a second comment stripper written as one regex.

#### Core-button-class ratchet (#1904)

`tests/Unit/CoreButtonClassRatchetTest.php` freezes, per file and per token, every WordPress core button class the plugin's own markup names — `button`, `button-primary`, `button-secondary`, `button-link`, `button-link-delete`, `button-small`, `button-large`, `button-hero`, `page-title-action` — and every `submit_button()` / `get_submit_button()` call, in `tests/fixtures/core-button-classes-baseline.php`. **It blocks at zero**: a core class that appears in our markup fails. Regenerate with `FFC_UPDATE_CORE_BUTTON_BASELINE=1 vendor/bin/phpunit --filter CoreButtonClassRatchet`. The scan (`tests/Support/CoreButtonClasses.php`) reads comment-stripped source for **class tokens**, not words: a `class="…"` value, the value given to a class (`'class' =>`, `$btn_class =`, `className =`, the class API), a literal made only of class tokens, and a token written as a selector. `type="button"`, `role="button"`, `FFC.button()` and prose never count, and a canary pins both sides. Its JS comment stripper ends a quoted string at its line, because a regex literal holding a quote would otherwise turn a later comment into code. The self-check is the independent recount, and because two readings agreeing on zero prove nothing it must also find the core buttons the excluded files print on purpose. `EXCLUDED` holds only those files — the core user screens and the `wp_die()` unsubscribe page — and an exclusion that stops printing one fails.

#### Native-dialog guard (#2534, #2535)

`tests/Unit/NativeDialogGuardTest.php` fails when a script under `assets/js/`, a PHP class under `includes/` or a template opens `alert()`, `confirm()` or `prompt()`, inline `onclick` included. Ask with `FFC.confirmDialog()` (its `reasonField` replaces `prompt()`), say a result with `FFC.adminNotice()`, `FFC.say()` or the screen's own notice, and carry a result across a reload with `FFC.reloadWithNotice()`; a link or button that only needs a yes carries `data-confirm` and ffc-core asks for it. It blocks at zero; its self-check injects a dialog into real files of each kind and compares the file list with a second traversal. It also fails when a dialog names an icon `Core\Icons` does not know. The scan is `tests/Support/NativeDialogs.php`.

#### Documentation-coverage guard (#1638)

`tests/Unit/DocumentationCoverageTest.php` fails when a Settings tab or a module has no documentation topic mapped to it, when a mapped topic is missing from the index, when the index lists a file that does not exist or links an anchor the file does not carry, and when a topic file on disk is never shown. The mapping is explicit (`TAB_TOPICS`, `MODULE_TOPICS`) because topics are named for what they explain, not for the tab. It proves a topic exists, never that it is right ("Documentation travels with the change" under "Contributing workflow"). Its self-check recounts the tab classes and the topic files on disk independently.

#### Deprecation-due guard (#1309)

`tests/Unit/DeprecationDueTest.php` fails when the plugin's own version reaches a recorded removal release, and fails when a WordPress deprecation call records none. It reads one marker, `@removal X.Y.Z`, written on the code that is still there — see "Deprecation cycles" in "Legacy and tech debt". Its self-check names the **oldest open** cycle, because that is the one a reader most needs to see the scan still reaching; re-point it when that cycle closes. That is maintenance the guard owes, not a defect.

#### Asset-handle guard (#1922)

`tests/Unit/AssetHandleUniquenessTest.php` fails when one file under `assets/` or `libs/js/` is enqueued or registered under two handles. WordPress de-duplicates by handle, never by file, so the file loads twice on a page that reaches both, and a script loaded twice runs twice. The scan (`tests/Support/AssetEnqueues.php`) reads tokens, normalises every suffix shape (`{$s}`, `{$ffc_s}`, `.min`, a vendored bundle's version constant) and resolves a handle from a literal or a class constant anywhere under `includes/`; a call whose handle it cannot read fails rather than being skipped, and the call count is recounted by a regex over comment-stripped code. `AssetRegistry`'s map is data, not calls, so the scan reads it too (`AssetEnqueues::registered()`). `ALLOWED` holds `ffc-admin.css` with its reason (see `.claude/rules/stylesheets.md` "Page scope on the admin `wrap`"). The converse holds as well (#1931): a handle declares its source in one class, because WordPress keeps the first registration and ignores the path and dependencies of every later one; it blocks at zero (`SHARED_DECLARATIONS` is empty).

#### Process-isolation guard (#2091)

`tests/Unit/ProcessIsolationScopeTest.php` fails when a test class runs every test in its own process (`@runTestsInSeparateProcesses`) with no reason in its source — an `alias:` or `overload:` mock, a `define()`, a namespaced function stub, `class_alias()` or `eval()` — and freezes the classes that do in `tests/fixtures/class-isolation-baseline.php`, which blocks at zero: a class that isolates every test is a decision to argue in the register. The single tests that keep their own process are frozen per file in `tests/fixtures/method-isolation-baseline.php`, each saying why in its own docblock beside the annotation. Both are ratchets both ways, regenerated with `FFC_UPDATE_ISOLATION_BASELINE=1 vendor/bin/phpunit --filter ProcessIsolationScope`. A test that reads process state (a `function_exists()` guard, a static memo) says so beside the annotation. Moving a test into the shared process is decided by the full suite, never by `--filter`.

Two traps. **PHPUnit reads an annotation anywhere in a docblock, prose included**, so a class docblock that only *names* the class-level annotation isolates the class; in prose, name it without its at-sign. And **`@runClassInSeparateProcess` runs one process per test in PHPUnit 9.6** just like `@runTestsInSeparateProcesses`, so it is refused in any test file and the counted spelling is used instead. The guard reads class and method docblocks as PHPUnit does, and its self-check recounts the method-level annotations by a second traversal.

#### Bootstrap-constant guard (#1806, #1809)

`tests/Unit/BootstrapConstantRedefinitionTest.php` fails when a PHP file under `tests/` — other than `tests/bootstrap.php` and `tests/Support/` — calls `define()` on a constant the bootstrap defines, and blocks at zero. Such a define never runs: the bootstrap runs first in the parent and again in every separate-process child. It **reads** the bootstrap's list from its tokens, so a constant the bootstrap gains is covered at once; it tokenizes every file, so a quoted `define()` is not one; and a `define()` whose name is not a string literal fails rather than being skipped. Its self-checks: the token scan of the bootstrap must equal an **executed** recount (the bootstrap run in a fresh PHP process, diffing the user constants), the scanned file list must equal a `scandir` recount, and a canary over synthetic source pins what counts as a call.

#### Fake-credential guard (#2637)

`tests/Unit/FakeCredentialStandardTest.php` fails when a literal given to a credential-like key (`password`, `smtp_pass`, `secret`, `api_key`, `*_KEY` / `*_SALT` constants, `--dbpass=`, `MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD:`), assigned to one (`$_POST['ffc_password'] = …`, a class constant named like one), returned by a stub of a function that hands one out (`wp_salt`, `wp_generate_password`) or typed into a password field by a JS test does not start with `fake-`, in the PHP and JS under `tests/` and `.github/scripts/` and in the workflows. The prefix makes "is this a real secret?" a mechanical answer. The named values live in `tests/Support/FakeCredentials.php`, mirrored by `tests/js/fake-credentials.js` (the guard holds the two equal), and the CI database and WordPress admin use the same ones. Three things it leaves alone on purpose: a value of three characters or fewer, which is the test's subject; a value read from a variable or a secret; and a record's link tokens (`magic_token`, `confirmation_token`). Like the identifier standard (`tests/Support/Identifiers.php`), it checks the value, not that a constant was used.


#### Instruction-file reference guard (#2869)

`tests/Unit/ClaudeRulesReferenceTest.php` reads `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/rules/*.md`, which no gate read before. It fails when a rule file declares no `paths:` (it would load in every session), when a glob in `paths:` matches no file in the repository (the rule would never load), when `CLAUDE.md` does not name a rule file, when a `` `file` "Section" `` reference — `→` chains included — in the instruction files, `includes/`, `tests/`, `templates/`, `assets/` or `.github/` names a heading or bold lead that file does not have, and when an instruction file quotes another file's section without naming the file. It blocks at zero. `docs/engineering/` is not scanned, because its files are verbatim snapshots. Its self-checks recount the rule files with `scandir()` and inject a broken reference into real text, which the scan must report. It sees presence, never truth: a reference to the right heading for the wrong reason passes.
### Config-level exclusions — `.claude/rules/lint-config.md`

The audited verdicts on rules switched off in `phpcs.xml.dist`, `phpstan.neon.dist`, `phpunit.xml.dist` and `.stylelintrc.json` (why `UnusedFunctionParameter`, `CommentedOutCode` and two Stylelint rules stay off, and why the `views/` carve-out is markup-only) are in `.claude/rules/lint-config.md`. It loads by itself when a session edits one of those files; **read it before switching a rule back on or widening an exclusion**.

### Test infrastructure

The rules for writing and debugging tests — the PHP and JS harness, jsdom, Patchwork and Brain\Monkey stubs and the order-dependence they cause, the pcov preload, clock reads, the coverage scope of `templates/` and the tab-indented `tests/` — are in `.claude/rules/tests.md`. It loads by itself when a session reads or edits a file under `tests/`; **read it before writing a test from anywhere else**. The two rules below stay here because they apply before every push and to product code.

- **Running the suite locally.** Install pcov once (`apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends php8.4-pcov`); the full suite is ~10 min. **The full run is required evidence only when the change can reach another file** — a stub added or removed (`Functions\when()`), a shared `tests/Support/` helper, a renamed identifier, or anything in `includes/`. That is what the order-dependence rule in `.claude/rules/tests.md` is scoped to: `--filter` is not evidence *there*. For a change that provably cannot pollute the process — a comment-only or assertion-message-only edit, where the token skeleton is byte-identical — the full local run buys nothing the `--filter` run and CI do not already give, and costs ~9 minutes per slice. Measured over the #1260 slices: two of four were comment-only and the full run found nothing in either. Do not skip it on the strength of *intent* — skip it on the strength of the skeleton diff being empty. Scope while iterating with `vendor/bin/phpunit --filter <Test>`; `vendor/bin/phpstan analyse --no-progress <path>` and `vendor/bin/phpcs --standard=phpcs.xml.dist -q <files>` (auto-fix with `vendor/bin/phpcbf`) reproduce the PHPStan/WPCS gates.
- **PHPStan/phpdoc idioms.** Put `@phpstan-type` on the **class** docblock (not the file docblock); consumers use `@phpstan-import-type X from Y` on their own class docblock. Avoid `@todo (` and other `@tag (` openings — phpdoc parses the `(` and errors; use prose instead.

### Build & assets

When editing assets that ship to the browser, rebuild the minified bundles so the matching `*.min.*` files stay in sync — the `Verify minified assets are up to date` CI job fails otherwise, including for a new `.min` that was never committed. No source map is built: none ships (`.distignore`), and `SCRIPT_DEBUG` serves the readable source, so a `sourceMappingURL` comment only pointed browsers at a file that is never there (#2344):

- **JS** → `npm run build:js` (regenerates `assets/js/*.min.js`).
- **CSS** → `npm run build:css` (regenerates `assets/css/*.min.css`).
- Both at once → `npm run build`.

---

## 3. Architecture and patterns

### Repository pattern (Reader/Writer split)

Data-access classes are split read-side vs write-side. Two shapes — pick by whether the repo needs multi-statement transactions:

- **Static repos (the common case).** Reads live in `*Reader`, writes in `*Writer`; both `use \FreeFormCertificate\Core\StaticRepositoryTrait` and return the **same** `cache_group()`, so a write invalidates the caches a read populated. **Callers call `*Reader::` / `*Writer::` directly — there is no façade.** The nine static façades (`CustomField`, `Audience`, `AudienceBooking`, `RecruitmentCall`/`Candidate`/`Notice`/`Adjutancy`/`Reason`, `ReregistrationSubmission`) were retired in #563 B3-A (#594). The row-shape `@phpstan-type` and any public constants (field-type lists, status sets, default colors, …) live **on the Reader** as the canonical home; consumers do `@phpstan-import-type … from …Reader`.
- **Instance repos.** `AppointmentRepository`, `SubmissionRepository`, `UrlShortenerRepository` are kept as thin façades that `extend AbstractRepository`, compose a `*Reader` + `*Writer` in the constructor, and expose the inherited generic CRUD. They are the **transactional aggregate root**: `begin_transaction()` → `FOR UPDATE` read → write → `commit()` run on the one shared global `$wpdb` the façade/reader/writer all bind. **Do NOT retire these into separate call sites** — that coherence is the whole point (deliberate B3-A decision; reiterated in each class's docblock).

**Legacy third shape — single-class instance repos (not a template for new code).** Four older classes `extend AbstractRepository` directly for the inherited generic CRUD + cache helpers (implementing only `get_table_name()` / `get_cache_group()`), with **no** `*Reader`/`*Writer` split and **no** transactions: `CalendarRepository`, `BlockedDateRepository` (`ffc_self_scheduling_*`), `FormRepository` (`wp_posts` metadata), `UserProfileRepository` (`ffc_user_profiles`, extracted from `UserManager`/`UserCreator` in #340). They are neither the static pattern nor transactional aggregate roots — they predate the static-default guidance and are **left as-is** (converting them to static would be pure namespace churn against the module-boundary baseline for zero functional gain). So the `extends AbstractRepository` census is 13 classes = these 4 + the 3 transactional façades + their 6 composed `*Reader`/`*Writer` halves. Don't cite these four as examples of the instance-façade pattern, and don't add new ones — new data-access code still follows the static default below.

When splitting or adding a repo, default to static; reach for the instance-façade only when callers need a read-modify-write transaction. **Test note:** a caller's alias mock that stubs both reads and writes must become **two** alias mocks — one on the `*Reader`, one on the `*Writer` — or the write call hits the real (un-mocked) class.

### Module bootstrap (per-module loaders)

Each feature module exposes a single bootstrap entry point — a `*Loader` class whose `init()` wires the module's runtime classes — so the orchestrator (`Loader::init_plugin()`) touches **one symbol per module** instead of newing-up its internals inline. This keeps `Loader` a thin composition root and narrows the `Root → <module>` dependency surface (#563 B3 coupling reduction). Current loaders: `AdminLoader`, `AudienceLoader`, `RecruitmentLoader`, `UrlShortenerLoader`, `ReregistrationLoader`, `SelfSchedulingLoader`, `DateMessagesLoader`.

Pattern: `init()` runs the module's wiring in its original order, gating admin-only pieces behind `is_admin()`; held-alive instances are kept as `protected` properties (so PHPStan doesn't flag them write-only); fire-and-forget `::init()` / one-shot `new` calls need no property. Pin the wiring with a `*LoaderTest` (overload/alias-mock the wired classes; assert each is constructed / `::init()`-ed) carrying `@covers`. The existing loader tests also carry a `class_exists()` pcov-preload in `setUp()`; a new one does not need it — see the pcov `class_exists()` preload rule in `.claude/rules/tests.md`.

**Only extract genuine module bootstrap.** A loader is worth it when the `Root → module` edge is *bootstrap wiring* (instantiating the module's runtime classes). It is NOT worth it when the edge is *orchestrator-level lifecycle* — role/capability registration & migration (`RoleRegistrar` / `CapabilityManager` / `CapabilityMigrator`), cron-event registration, or activation/upgrade `maybe_migrate()` — which legitimately belongs to the orchestrator. Extracting those into a "loader" would be indirection that narrows nothing (the bad-facade trap; see "Repository pattern" for the same principle).

**Shared script registration is not the orchestrator's either** (#1924). `Core\AssetRegistry` registers `ffc-core` (with `ffcCoreConfig`), the field behaviours, the front-end helpers (`ffc-rate-limit`), the captcha and the dynamic fragments, on the front end and at priority 1 of every admin request; `Loader` only calls its `init()`. **Every script more than one site enqueues lives in its `SCRIPTS` map too** (#1931) — path and dependencies, once — and a site names it with `AssetRegistry::enqueue_scripts( 'handle' )`, which registers the handle and the shared scripts it depends on before enqueuing, so it works before the registration hook has fired. WordPress keeps whichever registration comes first, so a source restated at each call site drifts in silence. A dependency only one screen needs (the form editor's field builder ahead of `ffc-admin-js`) is enqueued first by that screen, never added to the map. **Shared stylesheets follow the same rule** through `AssetRegistry::enqueue_styles( 'handle' )`, whose cases are literal `wp_enqueue_style()` calls rather than a map, because the stylesheet guards read the dependency graph off those calls. The palette stays `AssetHelper::enqueue_common_style()`, its single declaration, which the caller enqueues first. A stylesheet does not share a handle with a script of the same name — it takes a `-css` suffix (`ffc-audience-css`): the registries are separate, but one name for two files costs a lookup at every site.

**Documented exception — UserDashboard has no loader (deliberate, B3 phase 2).** Its only bootstrap wiring is a few `::init()` calls (`AccessControl`, `IdentifierLogin`, `UserCleanup`), left inline in `Loader`. The bulk of its `Root → UserDashboard` surface is capability/role lifecycle (`RoleRegistrar` / `CapabilityManager` / `CapabilityMigrator`) invoked from `Loader::register_ffc_roles_safe()` / `ensure_*_caps()` — orchestrator responsibility, not module bootstrap. A `UserDashboardLoader` would move those lines without shrinking the edge, so it was intentionally skipped.

### Shared-service module directories

A few `includes/` modules are small, single-purpose service buckets whose names are generic enough to invite drift. Keep each scoped to its stated purpose — do NOT let it become a "misc" drawer, since renaming to a crisper namespace later would ripple through the module-boundary baseline, every `use` / `@covers` / alias-mock and the autoloader for only a cosmetic gain (the same namespace-churn cost as any cross-module move). The guard is scope discipline, not a rename:

- **`services/` (`\Services`)** — user-centric query/identity services only (`UserService`, `UserIdentifiersQueryService`). A service that isn't about users belongs in its own domain module, not here.
- **`integrations/` (`\Integrations`)** — adapters to *external* systems (`EmailHandler` → SMTP, `IpGeolocation` → geolocation API). A class with no outbound/external dependency is not an integration.
- **`scheduling/` (`\Scheduling`)** — cross-cutting scheduling-domain services shared by the self-scheduling and audience features (`DateBlockingService`, `WorkingHoursService`, `IcsGenerator`, `SchedulingMailer`). Distinct from the `self-scheduling/` and `audience/` feature modules and from the "Scheduling" admin menu: feature UI/handlers go in those modules; only shared scheduling logic lives here.

### Form settings come from post meta — no plugin cache in front (#2241)

A form's settings (`_ffc_form_config`, `_ffc_form_fields`, the background) are read with `get_post_meta()`, through `FormRepository::getConfig()` / `getFields()` where a repository is in hand. **Do not put a plugin cache in front of them.** WordPress already caches post meta for the request and, with a persistent object cache, across requests, so a second copy saves no query and adds an invalidation duty: the plugin's own settings cache in `FormCache` was retired for exactly that (#2241, #2552). What stays in `FormCache` is the page-cache purge (`purge_page_cache()`, `purge_external_caches()`, `purge_all_pages()`), which is a different job: telling third-party page caches that the page embedding a form changed. The class keeps its name because a rename would ride every call site for nothing; the name is the known lie, recorded here.

### Email architecture (one pipeline — #662)

Every plugin-composed email flows through **one shared pipeline**; never hand-roll a chrome, a transport, or an inline body. When adding or touching an email:

1. **Compose the email body only** (the inner content). Resolve placeholders with `Core\TokenResolver::resolve()` (`{{token}}`) — never hand-rolled `str_replace`.
2. **Wrap in the single configurable chrome**: `EmailHelperTrait::ffc_email_document( $body, array( 'recipient' => $to ) )`. The chrome (header/body/footer/wrapper) is admin-configurable via `Core\EmailTemplateOptions` (the "Email Model" box, Settings → SMTP) and rendered by `templates/emails/layout.php` (table-based, inline styles for Gmail/Outlook). There is exactly **one** chrome — `SchedulingMailer::wrap_html` and the per-email cards were retired.
3. **Send through the chokepoint** `Core\EmailService::send()` (or `EmailHelperTrait::ffc_send_mail()`, which sets `text/html`). Never call `wp_mail()` directly. The global "disable all emails" kill-switch is enforced **inside** `EmailService::send()` — do **not** re-gate it caller-side.
4. **Default bodies live in files**, one per case, under `templates/emails/`. Return-array files (`return array( 'body' => __( … ) )`, loaded via the allowlisted `Core\EmailTemplates::load()` / `::body()`) for token/editable-default bodies; echo partials (via `ffc_render_email_partial()`) for handler-built ones. **Never build email HTML inline in a handler class** — extract it to a `templates/emails/*.php` file.
5. **Editable emails edit the body only, never the chrome.** Use `wp_editor` (TinyMCE) + a "Restore Default Text" button wired by the generic `assets/js/ffc-email-restore-default.js` (`data-editor` + `data-default-key`; default supplied via `wp_localize_script['ffcEmailRestoreDefaults']`). A message may still style its own **body cell** (background image, fallback and text colours, a text column) by passing `body_appearance` from `Core\EmailBodyAppearance::document_args()` to the layout (#1660); an empty appearance renders byte-for-byte as before, and the header and footer never take it.
6. **Surface the P5 notice**: `Core\EmailDisabledNotice::render()` at the top of any admin surface that edits an email.
